1 · The big picture — what are we building?

We are building a binary classifier: given a radar recording of someone walking, decide Parkinson's disease (PD) vs healthy control.

A radar sends a radio wave; it bounces off the moving body and comes back slightly changed. From that echo we build a picture of motion over time (a spectrogram). The whole project is about reading disease from that picture.

Why it matters: today PD screening is a specialist watching you walk in a clinic. Radar is contactless, private (no camera), needs no wearables, and could run continuously at home — flagging PD-like gait years earlier.

  • Control = healthy participant.
  • Prodromal = pre-symptomatic early PD (future data, ignore for now).

3 · How to read a spectrogram (the core skill)

Every recording is a picture with three things:

  • Horizontal axis = time (seconds, left → right).
  • Vertical axis = Doppler shift ≈ speed. Middle (0) = not moving toward/away; above 0 = moving toward the radar, below 0 = moving away. Further from the middle = faster.
  • Brightness = intensity — how much echo came back at that speed and moment.

The bright ribbon hugging the centre is the torso (slow, steady). The tall bursts reaching far up/down are the feet (each foot swing is fast). Read left-to-right and you're watching a "speed movie" of the walk.

One spike ≈ one step. Sign (up/down) = direction; height (distance from centre) = foot speed; spacing = rhythm.

4 · Doppler = speed, and what the spikes mean

The echo's frequency shift is proportional to how fast the reflecting part moved. At this radar (~13 mm wavelength): speed ≈ Doppler × 0.0065 m/s per Hz.

Doppler≈ speedwhat it is
~150–200 Hz~1–1.3 m/storso / walking speed (slow, steady)
~500 Hz~3.3 m/sa fast foot swing
~800 Hz~5.2 m/sthe maximum this radar can measure

That's why the torso sits at low Doppler (0–200 Hz) and the feet reach high Doppler (200–500 Hz). The energy of a spike tells you: how far it reaches = foot speed; how bright = strength of that motion; how regular = rhythm.

What is "log(1+intensity)"?

A display trick. Raw values span a huge range, so a plain plot would be all black with a few white dots. log(1+value) compresses the range so faint and strong features both show. The 1+ keeps zero mapping to zero. It changes how the image looks, not the data.

5 · Two radars: foot channel vs torso channel

There are radars aimed low (feet) and high (torso). ce_foot comes from the foot-aimed one — fast foot spikes dominate. ce_torso comes from the torso-aimed one — energy hugs 0 Hz. Neither perfectly isolates one body part (radar beams are wide), so you still see a faint torso band in ce_foot and vice versa. They emphasize different parts.

We feed the model both channels, because the paper shows the feet carry the timing signal, the torso the trunk motion, and their relationship is what breaks down in PD.

6 · What "ce" (contrast enhancement) does

ce = contrast-enhanced. The fast feet reflect far less energy than the big slow torso, so in the raw signal the foot spikes are faint. Contrast enhancement brightens the faint parts so the gait becomes visible.

Watch out: the enhancement is adaptive per recording — it rescales each trial to its own brightness. So you cannot compare absolute brightness between two ce images. (This is why the control-vs-PD image below can mislead.)

7 · The duration confound (why trial length lies)

We discovered PD participants take longer to finish a walk than controls — strongly in test1 (the chair stand-up), weakly in test2. That is a real difference, but a dangerous one: any feature that just adds up energy over time will look "discriminative" only because PD trials are longer, not because the gait differs.

The fix: cut every walk into fixed 3-second windows. A window is 3 s whether the trial was 9 s or 19 s — so trial length can no longer leak into the model. This is the single biggest design decision.

8 · Control vs PD — and why one image can fool you

Here is one control and one PD participant, cropped to a matched 6-second walking window, same colour scale.

What you can genuinely see: the PD panel shows the classic rhythmic "scalloped teeth" — each foot swing accelerates then decelerates, tracing an arc, one per step. That is textbook gait structure.

Why you must NOT conclude "PD feet are slower" from this:
  • Adaptive enhancement (section 6) rescaled these two recordings differently, so brightness/reach aren't comparable.
  • The control image is noisier (energy everywhere), which inflates its measured "foot reach" up toward the ±800 Hz hardware limit.
  • It's n = 1 per group — one person each. Individuals vary hugely.
Clinically healthy feet are expected to be faster (PD = bradykinesia), so the direction isn't crazy — but this single pair can't prove it.

9 · Levels of evidence & the real result

The lesson from section 8: eyeballing single images builds intuition but proves nothing. Trust rises as you climb this ladder:

LevelWhatTrust
One example pairlook at 1 control + 1 PD imageintuition only
Group averagesaverage many of each, comparemoderate
Confound-controlled statisticssubject-level LOSO + duration matching + permutation testthis is what you cite
The honest headline: once the duration confound is properly removed, there is a weak but statistically real PD signal (AUC ≈ 0.62–0.68, p = 0.022). It's the floor the deep-learning model must beat — and the reason the whole methodology exists.

10 · Reader's Q&A (follow-up questions)

Answers to questions raised while reading this guide. Each is self-contained.

Q1. How is a radar signal sent, received, and turned into a picture of motion?

The device. Each radar node is a small 24 GHz FMCW (Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave) unit: an Infineon BGT24MTR11 transceiver chip + an ADF4159 frequency synthesizer + microstrip antennas, controlled by a microcontroller, with the received signal digitized by an ADC.

Send & receive. The radar transmits a chirp — a radio wave whose frequency ramps up over ~625 microseconds. The wave reflects off the moving body; the receive antenna captures the delayed echo. The radar mixes the transmitted and received waves, producing a low-frequency beat signal whose frequency is proportional to the target's distance. The ADC samples that beat signal.

From echo to spectrogram (the chain):

  1. Range FFT — a Fourier transform across each chirp gives a range profile (how much reflection at each distance) over time. A 10 Hz high-pass filter removes static clutter (walls, furniture).
  2. Target integration — sum the distance-bins containing the person into one combined signal over time.
  3. STFT (Short-Time Fourier Transform) — slide a 50 ms window along that signal; at each instant compute the distribution of Doppler shifts (speeds). The result is the Doppler-vs-time matrix = the spectrogram.
  4. Magnitude + contrast enhancement → the ce_foot/ce_torso images you see.
chirp → echo → beat signal → range → integrate the person → STFT → Doppler-vs-time image.

Q2. Timed-Up-and-Go with a chair vs without?

TUG is a standard clinical mobility test. With chair (test1): start seated → stand up → walk ~3 m → turn → walk back → sit down — it includes the sit-to-stand and stand-to-sit transitions. Without chair (test2): start and end standing — just walk out, turn, walk back, no chair transitions.

Why it matters for us: the chair stand-up is slow and is where PD slowness shows most — but it is also where the duration confound is strongest (PD subjects take much longer to stand up). So test2 gives a cleaner gait comparison with less length bias.

Q3–Q5. How many radars? Are torso and feet the same signal? Why does the guide show them both "in one spectrogram" AND as "two separate spectrograms"?

This is the confusing part, so here it is precisely. There are two things called "foot/torso", at two different levels:

(1) Two radar groups → two separate images. The radar network has nodes aimed low (at foot height, ~0.15 m) and nodes aimed high (at the torso, ~1 m) — different mounting heights, all recording at the same time. The foot-aimed nodes are combined into one image, ce_foot; the torso-aimed nodes into another, ce_torso. So per trial we get two separate spectrogram images (this is what Section 5 shows).

(2) Two frequency bands → inside each single image. Because a radar beam is wide, even the foot-aimed image still catches the trunk. So within one image, the slow trunk appears as a band near 0 Hz and the fast feet as spikes at high Doppler. The bands are just different horizontal regions of the same picture — not separate files.

Both statements are true: we have 2 images per trial (ce_foot, ce_torso), and each image contains both a torso band and a foot band. ce_foot emphasizes the feet; ce_torso emphasizes the torso.

Q6. How many spectrograms in total?

SubjectsTrials (~6 each)Images (2 per trial)
Control33~198~396
PD25~150~300
Total58~348~696

Every trial produces exactly one ce_foot and one ce_torso — so half the images are foot-channel, half torso-channel. (When we later cut trials into 3 s windows, this becomes thousands of small window-images.)

Q7. How do we feed the model both radar spectrograms?

We stack them as channels, exactly like the red/green/blue layers of a colour photo. A colour image is 3 stacked layers (R, G, B); our input is 2 stacked layers: [ce_foot, ce_torso], each 224×224. The CNN's first layer reads all channels at once, so it can learn how the foot-radar view and the torso-radar view relate at the same instant.

Q8. What is the torso↔foot "relationship", and how does it "break down in PD"?

In healthy walking, the trunk's forward speed rises and falls in lock-step with the feet's heel-strikes — a tight, predictable coupling (you can even estimate heel-strike timing from the torso signal alone). The reference study found that in PD this coupling degrades: due to rigidity and altered postural control, the trunk no longer tracks the feet as cleanly.

That broken coupling is a physical PD signature — and why we feed both channels: a model seeing foot and torso together can detect that their relationship is off, which neither channel alone reveals.

Q9. What is the "gait" after contrast enhancement?

"Gait" = the walking pattern itself (the rhythmic foot/torso motion). Contrast enhancement does not change the gait — it changes how visible it is: it brightens the faint fast-foot spikes so the pattern stands out from the dark background, making it easier for a human (and a CNN) to read. Caveat: it rescales each recording separately, so it can also amplify that recording's noise.

Q10. The duration confound, once more

PD subjects finish the walk slower, so their recordings are longer. A feature like "total energy summed over the whole trial" is automatically bigger for a longer clip — so it looks "PD-discriminative" only because PD clips are longer, not because the gait differs. The model would then be secretly measuring clip length, not disease. That shortcut is the confound.

Q11. The fix: fixed 3-second windows

Instead of feeding a whole variable-length trial, we chop every trial into equal 3-second pieces. A window is 3 s whether it came from a 9 s or a 19 s trial — so length is constant across all inputs, and the model literally cannot use trial length as a cue. It must look at the gait pattern inside the window. (We then average the guesses over all of a subject's windows for one decision per person.)

This is the single biggest design decision because it removes the confound by construction — for free — instead of hoping the model ignores it.

Q12. "Confound-controlled statistics: subject-level LOSO + duration matching + permutation test" — in detail

  • LOSO (Leave-One-Subject-Out CV): train on 57 subjects, test on the 1 left out, repeat 58 times so every subject is tested by a model that never saw them. Stops the model from "recognising the person" instead of the disease (micro-Doppler encodes identity strongly).
  • Duration matching: build a subset where PD and control trials have the same distribution of durations, then re-run. If accuracy holds, the signal is not just length.
  • Permutation test: shuffle the PD/control labels randomly 1000× and re-run the whole pipeline each time to see the score achievable by chance. If the real score beats 95%+ of the shuffles (p<0.05), it is unlikely to be a fluke. Ours: p = 0.022.
"This is what you cite" = in the thesis you report these confound-controlled, LOSO, permutation-tested numbers — never a naive accuracy — because only these are defensible.

Q13. The confusion matrix we have

A 2×2 table of prediction vs truth over the 58 subjects (classical shape_clean baseline):

  • TP = PD correctly called PD = 16.
  • TN = control correctly called control = 22.
  • FP = control wrongly called PD (false alarm) = 11.
  • FN = PD wrongly called control (missed) = 9.

Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) = 16/25 = 0.64 (of real PD, how many we catch). Specificity = TN/(TN+FP) = 22/33 = 0.67 (of real controls, how many we clear). Both ~0.65 = weak, consistent with a modest signal.

Q14. The "honest headline": AUC 0.62–0.68, p=0.022, "the floor the deep model must beat"

  • AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) scores how well the model ranks a random PD above a random control: 0.5 = coin-flip, 1.0 = perfect. 0.62–0.68 = weak but above chance.
  • p = 0.022 (permutation) = only a 2.2% chance of this by luck → statistically real, not noise.
  • "Floor the deep model must beat" = this simple baseline is the minimum bar; the CNN should do better, and we trust it only if it beats this and passes the same confound checks.
  • "The reason the whole methodology exists" = all the careful design (windows, LOSO, matching, permutation) is what lets us make this honest, defensible claim instead of a fake-high number.

Q15. Reading the baseline AUC grid (model × feature-set heatmap)

Naming fix first: the heatmap you asked about is the baseline AUC grid (Section 9), not the confusion matrix. The confusion matrix is the 2×2 TP/TN/FP/FN table in Q13. This grid shows how well each model + feature-set combination separates PD from control.

The 3 models (rows):

  • logreg — logistic regression, a simple linear model.
  • svm_rbf — support-vector machine with an RBF kernel (non-linear).
  • random_forest — an ensemble of decision trees (non-linear).

The 5 feature sets (columns):

  • all_features — every handcrafted feature (clean and confounded mixed).
  • duration_invariant — features designed not to grow with trial length.
  • shape_clean — the strictest subset (|correlation with duration| < 0.3): the most honest, gait-shape-only features.
  • confounded_only — only the length-leaking energy-sum features (the "cheating" set, kept deliberately as a probe).
  • duration_only — a single feature: trial length itself. This is the confound floor — how much you get from duration alone.

How to read it — the findings:

  1. Everything is weak (~0.58–0.68). No model/feature-set is strong — a small, hard signal, as expected with 58 subjects.
  2. The duration floor is ~0.61 (logreg, duration_only). So raw all_features (0.63) and shape_clean (0.62) barely clear "just measure the clip length."
  3. confounded_only scores highest (logreg 0.68). The length-leaking features win — direct proof that much of the apparent signal is the duration confound, not gait.
  4. shape_clean (0.58–0.62) is the number to trust. It is the least inflated; logreg's 0.62 is the honest classical result, and it is this pipeline (residualized) that reached the significant p = 0.022.
  5. logreg ≥ svm/rf everywhere. The signal is simple / near-linear; fancier non-linear models do not help and can overfit tiny data.
  6. The two dark cells (svm 0.29, rf 0.45 under duration_only) are below 0.5 = worse than chance. That is an artifact, not a finding: with a single feature under LOSO, SVM probability calibration (and RF on 1-D) can invert the ranking on small folds. The trustworthy duration floor is logreg's 0.61 — ignore the sub-0.5 single-feature cells.
Read the grid left-to-right: shape_clean vs duration_only is the honest signal-vs-confound comparison, and confounded_only being the top score is the smoking gun that naive features cheat via trial length.
